newsitem.title: USA: Procter & Gamble, Regeneron in pact.
newsitem.headline: Procter & Gamble, Regeneron in pact.

text.p: Procter & Gamble Co. said Tuesday it has agreed to pay Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc. $135 million over five years as part of a collaboration agreement to develop and commercialize pharmaceutical products.
"This makes Regeneron much more viable in the next few years," said Kenneth Pounds, senior biotechnology analyst with Nutmeg Securities.
Regeneron's stock soared $4.02 to $11.89 on Nasdaq, where it was among the most active issues. Cincinnati-based P&G fell $1.25 to $132.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Over the first five years of the 10-year agreement, which is effective immediately, P&G will acquire up to $60 million in equity of Regeneron and provide $75 million in support of the Tarrytown, N.Y.-based biotechnology company's research efforts.
This includes the initial purchase of 4.35 million Regeneron shares for about $43 million at $9.87 per share and five-year warrants to purchase an additional 1.35 million shares at $9.87 per share.

P&G will buy more Regeneron shares in the second five years of the agreement, for a total stake of not more than 20 percent. The companies may choose to continue their collaboration, equally sharing all related research expenses.
The pact is in addition to $20 million in research funding that P&G agreed in December to provide to Regeneron to develop drugs for muscle diseases and disorders.

In return, P&G will have rights to Regeneron's current technology, which is expected to have applications in cardiovascular, bone, muscle, arthritis and other disease areas. P&G also will have rights to new technology developed as a result of the collaboration.

Regeneron is also in collaboration with Amgen Inc. to develop a treatment for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as ALS, or Lou Gehrig's disease. In January, the companies said the drug was ineffective when administered by regular, subcutaneous injection, sparking a sharp drop in Regeneron's stock price.

"There aren't any near-term prospects for drugs in the market after the failure. This makes it more likely that the company will survive to a day that they will have a drug on the market." said Pounds of Nutmeg Securities.
"Now Regeneron can expand research efforts. With expansion, the odds of hitting a homerun in about five years are increased -- but it doesn't improve the odds to a huge extent."
